Each block proved live under its neighbor's "eventually" does not make the pair live. A liveness assumption is never violated at any particular cycle, so there is no first violation to start an induction from, and the circle proves nothing. The ring of the example never starts. Break the circle with a liveness argument that does not depend on the other block, such as a bounded response proved for one of them, or prove the composition directly.
:::

**Pitfalls.** The liveness ring. Fairness assumptions in a mutual liveness argument are the same trap in another form (@sec-ch19-fairness). And the safety rule needs a register in every loop. Two blocks whose guarantees depend on each other in the same cycle, through combinational paths, form a circle with no delay to induct over; the argument that justified block A does not apply, and this book has no example of the tool's behavior on such a ring.

### Case split {#sec-ch19-casesplit}

This entry runs on a design outside the chapter's three, a multiplier checked two ways, because a case split pays only where the cases shrink a hard solver problem, and the FIFO, the handshake and the DMA have no such datapath. It is also a preview of the equivalence chapter, *Equivalence, Structural and Static Verification*.

**Problem.** One solver problem is too hard to solve whole.

**Idea.** Prove the property under each of several conditions that together cover every case, and prove that they do. McMillan's case splitting in compositional model checking splits on the value of a variable, and its soundness rests on the cases ranging over every value [@mcmillan1999compositional].

**How to write it.** One session per case, with the case as an assumption, and one more session for the completeness check, an assertion that the disjunction of the case conditions always holds. The miter compares the multiplication operator with a shift-and-add loop; a parameter plants a bug that only one case in four can show:

```{.systemverilog include="examples/ch19-formal-techniques/case-split/mul.sv" lines="7-19"}
```

**What it preserves.** Proofs, if every case is proved and the completeness check is proved. On a case condition over a free input, as here, completeness is a tautology; on state, it is an invariant to prove.

**Example.** `case-split/`, in-house engines, at eight bits:

```{.text include="examples/ch19-formal-techniques/case-split/run.out"}
```

The whole miter is proven; so is each of the four cases on the top two bits of `a`, and so is the completeness check. With the bug planted, the case `a[7:6] == 3` fails at depth 0, the depth of a design with no registers. Then the trap: a case list that forgot case 3 would pass all three of its cases, which block B proved and which the bug, living only in case 3, does not touch; only the completeness check, which fails at depth 0, says that the list is short. @tbl-ch19-seconds gives the time of each run: the four cases cost about as much in total as the whole, so on this design a split pays only if the cases run in parallel.

**Pitfalls.** The forgotten case, which proves nothing and prints only `proven` rows unless the completeness check is run. And a split that does not shrink the hard part: if every case still contains the whole difficulty, each case is as slow as the whole.

### Hierarchical proof {#sec-ch19-hier}

**Problem.** A parent built from children, each of which has been proved. Proving the parent flat repeats every child's proof inside a larger model.

**Idea.** Box each child, and assume of it the contract proved on it. This is the black box of @sec-ch19-bbox with the contract that removes its spurious traces, the ghost state of @sec-ch19-ghost that lets the contract be stated on ports, and the assume-guarantee of @sec-ch19-ag that makes the circle sound.

**How to write it.** The pipe of two FIFOs in `hier.sv` moves a word from the first to the second whenever the first has one and the second has room, and counts the words it holds in a ghost `G` from its own ports. The script boxes the inner `fifo` module, which leaves each `fifo_ctr` wrapper and its ghost `g` in the model, and assumes the contract of each child:

```{.tcl include="examples/ch19-formal-techniques/hier/hier.tcl" lines="9-27"}
```

`P1_A` says the pipe is empty when `G` is zero; `P2_A` that when the pipe is full, `G` is at least `DEPTH`.

**What it preserves.** Proofs, if each contract is proved on its block under that block's own input assumptions, and those input assumptions are proved as assertions in the parent.

**Example.** `hier/`, in-house engines, at 16 entries:

```{.text include="examples/ch19-formal-techniques/hier/run.out"}
```

With both children boxed under the full contract, neither parent property gets a verdict from induction in five seconds; the cover of both children full is reached at depth 33. With half the contract, only "empty exactly when `g` is zero", `P2_A` fails at depth 1: the boxed FIFO raises `full` while its `g` is below `DEPTH`, which the missing half would have forbidden. Block C is the step that makes the proof go. The parent's own helper says that `G` is the sum of the two ghost counts, each at most `DEPTH`. It is proven, and with it assumed both parent properties are proven; `Drain_C`, a word in and out again, is `P1_A`'s witness, reached at depth 4. The contracts are proved in `contract/` (@sec-ch19-ghost) at 16 and at 64 entries. The comparison is the example `hier-ric3/`, which needs rIC3:

```{.text include="examples/ch19-formal-techniques/hier-ric3/run.out"}
```

rIC3 proves both properties without the parent helper, boxed and flat. The honest finding is that boxing alone did not make the parent cheaper for the in-house engine: the parent's properties read counters and flags, not the memories, and the tool's reduction of the model to the logic the properties can see may already have left the memories out. This book did not check whether it did. What the contracts bought is that the parent's helper could be stated on ports at all, and that the proof of the parent no longer depends on anything inside a child.

**Pitfalls.** A contract that names a child's internal signal, such as its `count`, cannot be assumed once the child is boxed, because the signal is no longer in the model; state contracts on ports and on ghost state built from ports. And half a contract gives spurious counterexamples that look like parent bugs, as block B shows.

### Property decomposition on the DMA {#sec-ch19-decomp}

**Problem.** An end-to-end property of a design with hundreds of state bits. On the DMA: when channel 0 finishes without error, it has had as many write responses as the length it was started with.

**Idea.** Replace the end-to-end property by a chain of local lemmas, each closer to the logic that keeps it, and check that the end-to-end property follows from the lemmas.

**How to write it.** Ghost state bound into the DMA records the length when the channel starts and counts the write responses since:

```{.systemverilog include="examples/ch19-formal-techniques/decomp/dma_wcount.sv" lines="4-24"}
```

The property `E2E_A` compares the two when the channel finishes without error. The lemma `L1` says that responses so far plus the words still to write equal the length, always; `L2` that when the channel finishes without error, no words are left. They are typed once and asserted or assumed:

```{.tcl include="examples/ch19-formal-techniques/decomp/decomp.tcl" lines="11-13"}
```

**What it preserves.** Proofs, if the end-to-end property follows from the lemmas, which is itself a proof to run, and each lemma is proved without assuming the end-to-end property or a lemma whose own proof assumed it.

**Example.** `decomp/`, in-house engines:

```{.text include="examples/ch19-formal-techniques/decomp/run.out"}
```

Alone, none of the three properties gets a verdict in five seconds from any of the three engines: bounded search finds no counterexample, and induction and IC3 find no proof. The witness cover, a channel finishing a three-word transfer without error, is reached at depth 15. With the two lemmas assumed, the end-to-end property is proven by induction.

So the chain is sound and its last link is easy. The first links are where the work is. Neither lemma is proved here, and neither is refuted: a bounded search that finds no counterexample within its limit has not shown a lemma true. Each is a statement about counters that the DMA updates in several places, and induction on such a statement fails for the reason the previous chapter's pointer property failed: its counterexamples to induction may start from combinations of internal state that no trace from reset reaches. Proving the lemmas would take a layer of invariants of the DMA itself, facts of the kind "a write in flight implies the channel is busy", each a helper with its own proof. @fig-ch19-decomp draws the chain with its verdicts. The next layer is left to the reader as a project: it is real verification work on a real block, and this chapter does not pretend it is done. Lemmas that together imply the end-to-end property are the aim, not a defect: `L1` and `L2` imply `E2E_A` with no design involved, which is why induction proves it at once.

![The decomposition of the DMA's end-to-end property, with the verdicts of the `decomp` example. The end-to-end property is proven from the two lemmas; the lemmas, alone, have no verdict from any engine in five seconds; below them, the layer of DMA invariants they would need, not written.](../figures/ch19-decomp.svg){#fig-ch19-decomp fig-alt="A tree with three levels. At the top, E2E_A, shaded green and labeled proven with L1 and L2 assumed. Below it, two nodes L1 and L2, hatched and labeled no verdict in 5 s by bmc, kind and ic3. Below them, a dashed box labeled invariants of the DMA, for example a write in flight implies busy, not written. Beside the top node, the witness cover Done3_C, covered at depth 15."}

::: {.callout-tip title="In Practice"}
Decomposition pays when each local property is inductive, or nearly so: a fact one step of the design shows, or one helper away from it. Before splitting a property, write the lemmas and run induction on each with a short limit. A lemma that is true and not inductive has not removed the difficulty; it has moved it, and the decomposition is only as far along as its least inductive lemma.
:::

**Pitfalls.** Lemmas that are not inductive move the difficulty without reducing it; the DMA's two are unproved, as above. And a chain is circular when a lemma's proof assumes the end-to-end property, or another lemma whose proof assumed it: draw which proof assumed which property and check that the graph has no cycle. The circular form of @sec-ch19-ag is not an exception here, even when the loop passes through registers. It is sound because each block is proved alone and assumes only what arrives at its inputs, while lemmas about one design are proved on the same state, so an assumed lemma can remove the very traces on which the lemma it helps would fail. Block E of `ag/` is the warning: two false lemmas about a ring of two registers, each reset to 1, are each proven with the other assumed. Their witness covers happen to be unreachable there, but a cover is not a reliable guard against this mistake; the acyclic proof graph is.

## Constraining and bug hunting {#sec-ch19-constrain}

The fifth family changes the assumptions or the question to reach an answer sooner. Five of its six entries are owned by the previous chapter, which defined assumptions, bounded proof, covers and liveness; each entry here is compact and says what it preserves and where it is taught in full.

### Environment assumptions {#sec-ch19-envassume}

**Idea.** State what the inputs may legally do, so that the engine examines only legal traffic. @sec-ch18-assume defined an assumption as a conjunct of every query and showed what an over-constraint does to a report.

**What it preserves.** Proofs, for every environment that keeps the assumptions, and for no other.

**Where it is taught.** @sec-ch18-assume. This chapter adds where assumptions should come from and where they go: write them from the interface rules of the specification, ideally as the receiver-role half of a protocol checker (@sec-ch19-protocol), and discharge each as an assertion on the neighbor that drives the signals (@sec-ch19-ag). An assumption with no named block that guarantees it is an unchecked claim about the world.

### Over-constraint for hunting {#sec-ch19-overconstrain}

**Idea.** Restrict the inputs on purpose, to steer a search toward a deep bug: hold a mode fixed, forbid back-pressure, allow only one requester. The search is smaller and reaches deeper within the same limit.

**What it preserves.** Counterexamples only. A trace found under the restriction is a trace of the design; a `proven` under it is a statement about the restricted environment.

**Where it is taught.** @sec-ch18-assume, whose run under `assume {!req}` proved a false assertion. A hunting script should print no `proven` a reader could take for a proof: name it as a hunt, select a bounded engine, which cannot report a proof (@sec-ch18-bmc), and keep it apart from the sign-off regression.

### Bounded proof with a depth argument {#sec-ch19-bounded}

**Idea.** Run a bounded search to some depth $N$ and argue that $N$ is enough.

**What it preserves.** Counterexamples, and a proof only to depth $N$. It equals a full proof only if $N$ reaches a completeness threshold, which is as hard to know as the answer.

**Where it is taught.** @sec-ch18-bmc, which defined the completeness threshold and the bounded result worth recording: a bound together with the depth of the deepest behavior of interest. The usual industrial argument, that every cover of interest is reached within the bound, is evidence and not proof. InFormal's report prints no bound for a bounded search [@informal-tool], so the tool offers no bounded proof as a feature; a time limit that expires says nothing about depth.

### Cover-guided deep search {#sec-ch19-guided}

**Idea.** Reach a deep state with a cover, then start a new search from that state, so that a bug a further $N$ cycles on needs an unrolling of $N$, not of the whole distance.

**What it preserves.** Counterexamples: the start state is reachable because a trace from reset reached it.

**Where it is taught.** Nowhere in full: this book read no peer-reviewed source for it, and InFormal has no such feature. Its sound cousin is the initial-value abstraction of @sec-ch19-initval, which starts from a whole set of states and proves the side conditions that make the set safe to start from.

### Bounded liveness {#sec-ch19-boundedlive}

**Idea.** Replace "eventually" by "within $N$ cycles". The bounded form is a safety property, with finite counterexamples, and every engine handles it.

**What it preserves.** It is a stronger property: a proof of the bounded form proves the eventual one, and a counterexample to the bounded form may be a latency, not a deadlock.

**Where it is taught.** @sec-ch18-liveness. On the handshake, the last block of `cut-timer/` proves that a request taken while idle is granted within 201 cycles, refutes the 200-cycle version at depth 201, and shows the bounded form failing under the timer abstraction, because the free `expired` need never rise:

```{.text include="examples/ch19-formal-techniques/cut-timer/run.out" lines="95-104"}
```

A property that names a delay needs the logic that makes the delay.

### Fairness {#sec-ch19-fairness}

**Idea.** Assume that something happens infinitely often, so that liveness counterexamples in which the environment stalls for ever are excluded.

**What it preserves.** Proofs of liveness, for environments that are fair in the stated sense.

**Where it is taught.** @sec-ch18-liveness. This chapter adds one observation from @sec-ch19-ag. A fairness assumption about a neighbor, used in a liveness argument whose neighbor in turn assumes fairness of this block, is the circular liveness case, and it is unsound in the same way: the ring of the example satisfies each block's fairness assumption only if the other block's guarantee already holds. And a fairness assumption is checked by refutation, not by a cover. A cover is a finite trace, and a finite trace is reached even when no infinite run satisfies the assumption, in which case every liveness assertion is proven. Assert something that can never happen eventually, `s_eventually 1'b0`, under the assumption and expect a counterexample: block C of @sec-ch19-ag refutes it at depth 4, a fair lasso, beside its proof.

## Trusting the result {#sec-ch19-trust}

The last family changes nothing about the problem. It asks of a finished proof whether it could have failed: whether the assumptions left the design room to misbehave, and whether the properties would have noticed if it had.

### Witness cover {#sec-ch19-witness}

**Idea.** Every assertion ships with a cover of the situation it is about, run under the same assumptions.

**What it preserves.** Not applicable; it is a check on the setup.

**Where it is taught.** @sec-ch18-cover, which defines a witness as a cover of the case the assertion is about. Wherever an example of this chapter proves an implication, a witness cover runs beside it, under the same assumptions, and its trace passes through the antecedent, as the grant at depth 202 passes through the rise of `busy` in @sec-ch19-bbox. A cover of the antecedent alone is not always enough. The witness must run at least to the last cycle in which the assertion's consequent is judged, since an assumption can let the antecedent happen and then leave no trace that reaches the consequent's cycle. For a ranged consequent that is the cycle in which the consequent is satisfied, or the end of the range: the arbiter's witnesses in @sec-ch19-symmetry run to the end of the four cycles, `req[i] && !gnt[i] ##4 1`, and the handshake's grant within 201 cycles has the grant itself as its witness. On this tool the witness must also run to the end of any multi-cycle assumption's window (@sec-ch19-timer). Every proved implication in the examples has a reached witness that meets this minimum (@sec-ch19-preserve lists the exceptions: the vacuous demonstrations and the timed reruns). The minimum is necessary, not sufficient: the witness must also reach the case the assertion exists to check, and the next entry shows a cover that meets the minimum reached beside a vacuous proof. The tool flags no vacuity on its own: a proved assertion whose antecedent can never occur reads `proven` like any other. The witness covers of this chapter's examples are the evidence that each proved implication had something to say.

### Assumption sanity {#sec-ch19-sanity}

**Problem.** Assumptions that leave the design no room to fail. @sec-ch18-assume showed contradictory assumptions and a dead end that every trace runs into. The harder case is a dead end that only some traces meet.

**Idea.** Check with covers that the environment can run on for a long time, and with a witness cover for each assertion that the assertion's own scenario survives the assumptions. The exact condition, that every reachable state satisfying the assumptions has a successor that satisfies them too, is a statement about all paths branching from each state, and SVA, a language about single traces, cannot express it. Covers can show only that some traces of the kind wanted exist.

**How to write it.** A free-running cycle count with a deep cover, `Deep_C`, and a witness cover per assertion, `Witness_C`. The design is a counter with a mode chosen by an input in the first cycle after reset:

```{.tcl include="examples/ch19-formal-techniques/sanity/sanity.tcl" lines="8-12"}
```

**What it preserves.** Not applicable.

**Example.** `sanity/`, in-house engines:

```{.text include="examples/ch19-formal-techniques/sanity/run.out"}
```

With no assumption, the false assertion is refuted at depth 10 and both covers are reached. Under an assumption that every trace runs into, the counter must never reach 5, the assertion is proven and both covers are unreachable: the generic check works. Under an assumption that only mode-1 traces run into, the assertion is proven, the deep cover is reached at depth 51, because mode-0 traces run on, and only the witness cover is unreachable. The assertion is about mode 1, and in mode 1 no trace survives long enough to test it.

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall"}
A generic deep cover, "time keeps passing", does not detect a dead end that only some traces meet. In part C above it is reached at depth 51 while the proved assertion is vacuous. Only the assertion's own witness cover, under the final assumptions, shows the problem, and only if it is chosen for the case the assertion checks. The consequent of `A_mode` is judged in its antecedent's cycle, so a cover of the antecedent alone, `mode && chosen`, already runs to the last cycle judged; it is reached, since mode 1 is chosen a cycle or two after reset and the dead end comes only at 5, and it would have passed this vacuous proof. Write a witness cover for each assertion that reaches the case the assertion exists to check, here mode 1 with the counter about to reach 9, and at least runs to the last cycle the consequent is judged in (@sec-ch19-witness); read an unreachable one as a failure of the proof, not as a curiosity. The boundary matters too: `Witness_C` stops at 8, so an assumption that ended mode-1 traces at 9 itself would leave it reached, and only a cover that runs on into the cycle in which the counter could be 9, `mode && chosen && cnt == 4'd8 ##1 1`, would catch that.
:::

**Pitfalls.** The middle case above, where the generic check passes and the per-assertion check is the only one that fails. And contradictory assumptions, which the tool accepts without a message (@sec-ch18-assume): every assertion is then proven and every cover unreachable, so a regression with no covers reports a perfect result.

### Mutation of the design {#sec-ch19-mutation}

**Problem.** A property set that cannot fail. Witness covers show that the assertions' scenarios occur; they do not show that the assertions would notice a bug in them.

**Idea.** Plant a bug and run the property set; some property must fail. A mutant that survives every property is either a gap in the property set or an equivalent mutant, one that changes the design without changing its behavior. Mutation as a test-quality measure goes back to DeMillo, Lipton and Sayward [@demillo1978mutation]. Chockler, Kupferman, Kurshan and Vardi applied the idea to model checking, measuring the coverage of a specification by which small changes to the design make it fail [@chockler2001practical]. The method in full belongs to the chapter *Mutation Testing: Qualifying the Testbench*.

**How to write it.** A procedure that applies one `sed` edit to a copy of the design when the script runs, so that the mutant cannot drift from the design it mutates, and fails if the edit matched nothing. The property set is the FIFO checker of @sec-ch09-example, bound as it ships, the previous chapter's pointer property `EmptyPtrs_A`, and the tracked-word check of @sec-ch19-track.

**What it preserves.** Not applicable; a killed mutant is evidence that the property set can fail.

**Example.** `mutants/`, in-house engines, a two-second bounded search for each property on each of three mutants, and one longer run where a counterexample lies just past two seconds: a read pointer that stays put when a push and a pop meet, a count that wraps one push short of full, and a read pointer that steps by two. The summary the script prints last:

```{.text include="examples/ch19-formal-techniques/mutants/run.out" lines="56-69"}
```

Every mutant is killed, but not by the same properties. The occupancy checker of @sec-ch09-example kills only the mutant that breaks the count; the two mutants that corrupt data without disturbing occupancy pass all of its assertions within the limit. The tracked-word check kills both data mutants within two seconds; on the count mutant its first failure is at depth 17, which a search reaches only a few seconds in, so the script runs it alone with thirty seconds, where it kills that mutant too. The pointer property kills all three. No single property would have been enough, and the occupancy checker alone, which a team might take for a FIFO's complete property set, misses both data bugs.

**Pitfalls.** A mutant that survives because the property set is vacuous under the assumptions, which is why mutation and witness covers go together. Equivalent mutants, which no property can kill and which have to be argued away by hand. And the time limit: "no counterexample in two seconds" is a statement about a bounded search, not a survival.

### Cone-of-influence and proof-core coverage {#sec-ch19-core}

**Idea.** Ask which logic the proofs depended on. The cone of influence of a property, all the logic that can affect it, over-reports: much of it may be logic the proof never needed. A proof core, the part of the design that a particular proof actually used, is tighter. McMillan and Amla's *Automatic Abstraction without Counterexamples* uses the logic that a bounded proof, the solver's proof that no counterexample exists to some depth, needed [@mcmillan2003abstraction]; Ghassabani, Gacek and Whalen's *Efficient Generation of Inductive Validity Cores for Safety Properties* computes such cores for inductive proofs [@ghassabani2016ivc]. Cadence describes a coverage app for its Jasper platform that measures checker coverage with proof cores; that is the vendor's statement [@cadence-jasper-cov].

**What it preserves.** Not applicable; it measures the property set.

**Where it is taught.** Not available in InFormal at the pinned commit [@informal-tool]; described only. The chapter *Metrics, Closure and Sign-off* returns to formal coverage as part of a closure argument.

::: {.callout-tip title="In Practice"}
A proof that goes into a sign-off review should travel with three things. The first is a witness cover for each assertion, reached under the final assumptions, abstractions and black boxes, not under an earlier setup. The second is at least one planted bug that the property set kills, applied by script to the shipped design so that it cannot drift. The third is the record: the engine and its limit, the parameter values, each black box and cut, and each assumption, with the side condition that justifies it and where that side condition was discharged. A reviewer who has these can re-run the argument; a reviewer who has only the word `proven` cannot.
:::

## Six recipes {#sec-ch19-recipes}

The catalog's entries combine into checks that teams run on every chip. Six of them have names of their own, and commercial tools sell each as an application. Each recipe below is one page: the question, the entries it combines, the assertion pattern in words, what it preserves, and the chapter that carries it further. None is run in this chapter; the recipes are prose, and each names where the book measures it.

### Connectivity {#sec-ch19-conn}

**Question.** Does each signal at one block's port reach the right port of another block, under the right condition and with the right delay?

**Entries.** Black box (@sec-ch19-bbox) every IP block, so that only the wiring between them is left in the model; environment assumptions (@sec-ch19-envassume) for the mode and configuration inputs; one assertion per row of a connection table, of the form "when the condition holds, the destination equals the source", or the same after a fixed delay for a pipelined path. A script that reads the table and emits one assertion per row is the whole method. On the DMA, the interrupt output is a registered combination of each channel's enable, done and error bits, and its connection table has one row per channel term, from that channel's bits to the interrupt.

**Preserves.** Proofs survive the boxes; a counterexample that runs through a box is spurious and names a box to open or a contract to add.

**Further.** Cadence and Synopsys each sell a connectivity application; Cadence's, by its own description, reads the connection specification from a comma-separated file or an IP-XACT description [@cadence-jasper-conn; @synopsys-vcformal-datasheet]. The full flow belongs to *Equivalence, Structural and Static Verification*.

### Register access {#sec-ch19-regs}

**Question.** Does every register read back what was written, honor its access type and come out of reset with its documented value?

**Entries.** Symbolic constants (@sec-ch19-symconst) for the address and the data, so that one property covers every register and every value; ghost state (@sec-ch19-ghost), a copy of the symbolic register written when the bus writes it; the bus protocol's rules assumed (@sec-ch19-protocol). The assertion: a read of the symbolic address, with no write to it since the last write, returns the ghost copy, masked by the register's access type. On the DMA, the source address register drops its two low bits by design, so the read-back assertion compares against the written value with those bits cleared, a fact the register description states and the property must repeat.

**Preserves.** Both, since symbolic constants and ghost state are exact.

**Further.** Both vendors describe register-checking applications, which by their own descriptions check access types and reset values; Cadence's takes the register description as a comma-separated file or an IP-XACT description [@cadence-jasper-csr; @synopsys-vcformal-datasheet]. The flow belongs to *Equivalence, Structural and Static Verification*, and register models to *Registers and Reuse*.

### X-propagation {#sec-ch19-xprop}

**Question.** Can an unknown value, from a register without reset or an undriven input, reach an output or a control point?

**Entries.** A solver's model is two-valued (@sec-ch17-smt), and InFormal's front end drops a module that calls `$isunknown` (@sec-ch09-tools), so the tool cannot represent an unknown directly. The recipe is the book's own construction, by self-composition (@sec-ch19-infoflow): two copies of the design with every ordinary input shared and every source of an unknown free and independent in each copy. An output that can differ between the copies is an output an unknown can reach. Initial-value freedom (@sec-ch19-initval) supplies the unreset registers.

**Preserves.** A difference between the copies is an output whose value depends on the value an unknown takes, which is real in silicon as well; whether it is a bug depends on whether the output is used in that cycle.

**Further.** Both vendors describe applications for unknown-value propagation [@cadence-jasper-xprop; @synopsys-vcformal-datasheet]. The flow belongs to *Equivalence, Structural and Static Verification*, with the simulation semantics of X that @sec-ch04-fourstate introduced.

### Unreachable-coverage analysis {#sec-ch19-unreach}

**Question.** A coverage point that simulation never hit: can it be hit at all?

**Entries.** Restate the point as a cover (@sec-ch18-cover). An unreachable cover is a proof, so the point can be excluded from the coverage goal with a reason a reviewer can check, as @sec-ch08-closure asks of every exclusion.

**Preserves.** Unreachable *under the assumptions in force*. An over-constraint makes points unreachable that real traffic can hit, so an exclusion from a formal run is an exclusion only for environments that keep its assumptions; it should carry them.

**Further.** Both vendors describe applications for this [@cadence-jasper-cov; @synopsys-vcformal-datasheet]. The flow belongs to *Metrics, Closure and Sign-off*.

### Information flow by self-composition {#sec-ch19-infoflow}

**Question.** Can a secret input influence a public output?

**Entries.** Two copies of the design in one wrapper, from the same reset, with public inputs tied together and secret inputs free and independent; an assertion that the public outputs are equal in every cycle. The pair property is a property of two traces at once, which Clarkson and Schneider call a hyperproperty [@clarkson2010hyperproperties]; self-composition turns it into an ordinary safety property of the product, the observation of Barthe, D'Argenio and Rezk's *Secure Information Flow by Self-Composition* and of Terauchi and Aiken's *Secure Information Flow as a Safety Problem* [@barthe2004selfcomposition; @terauchi2005safety]. Every engine of @sec-ch18-engines applies to the product. On the DMA, a candidate is that a read of one channel's status does not depend on the other channel's registers.

**Preserves.** Both, for the modeled design, cycle by cycle. Timing differences in cycles are caught; physical channels are not modeled.

**Further.** The flow, and security properties in general, belong to *Safety and Security Verification*.

### Clock-gating equivalence {#sec-ch19-clockgate}

**Question.** Does the design with clock gating inserted behave as the design without it?

**Entries.** A miter (@sec-ch19-casesplit used one): both versions in one wrapper, inputs shared, same reset, outputs asserted equal. The miter is built by hand, as a wrapper. The gated register is written as a register with an enable, against the original; how the tool models a clock derived from a gate was not measured for this book, so the recipe keeps the gating at the level of an enable. Sequential equivalence checkers exploit the structural similarity of the two versions, as in van Eijk's *Sequential Equivalence Checking Based on Structural Similarities* [@vaneijk2000sec].

**Preserves.** Both, for the outputs compared.

**Further.** Both vendors list clock-gating checks among the uses of their sequential equivalence applications [@cadence-jasper-sec; @synopsys-vcformal-datasheet]. The flow belongs to *Equivalence, Structural and Static Verification*.

## Worked example: a pipe of two 256-entry FIFOs {#sec-ch19-example}

The pipe of @sec-ch19-hier, at 256 entries per FIFO. It has two control properties: `P1`, the pipe is empty when its count `G` is zero, and `P2`, when the pipe is full, `G` is at least 256. The two memories alone hold 4,096 bits, and the deepest behavior the properties are about, the pipe full, is more than five hundred cycles from reset. The procedure is the previous chapter's (@sec-ch18-example), with the techniques of this chapter inserted where the engines stop. Every property and assumption is typed once:

```{.tcl include="examples/ch19-formal-techniques/pipe-256/pipe.tcl" lines="14-20"}
```

Before reading on, predict each step's verdict: the covers by bounded search on the boxed pipe; the child's contract by induction, with and without its ghost helper; induction on the parent with both children boxed; the parent's helper; the parent's properties under it; a mutant child.

**Step 1, covers.** On the boxed pipe, under the children's contracts, by bounded search:

```{.text include="examples/ch19-formal-techniques/pipe-256/run.out" lines="1-12"}
```

`Full_C`, the pipe full, is `P2`'s antecedent and its natural witness. It is 513 cycles deep, and step 6 gives its bounded search two minutes, four times the first look's limit; so the first look uses shallow witnesses, chosen for the budget, and the deep one runs once, under the final assumptions. `Drain_C`, a word in and out again, is `P1`'s witness and is reached at depth 4; `Both1_C`, a word in each child, exercises both terms of the helper to come, at depth 3; `U1Full_C`, the second child full, shows that the boxed model can reach a full child under the contract, at depth 258. Together they show that the contracts leave the pipe room to move, fill and drain. On the 16-entry pipe of @sec-ch19-hier, `Both_C`, both children full and so the first child's `full` high by its contract, is reached at depth 33, and 33 is twice 16 plus one, which predicts the 513 of step 6.

**Step 2, the child's contract.** At 256 entries, on one FIFO with its ghost count, the contract of @sec-ch19-ghost is proven with the ghost helper assumed, and the helper is proven alone:

```{.text include="examples/ch19-formal-techniques/pipe-256/run.out" lines="13-21"}
```

**Steps 3 and 4, box and induct.** Both children boxed, their contracts assumed, induction on the parent:

```{.tcl include="examples/ch19-formal-techniques/pipe-256/pipe.tcl" lines="80-86"}
```

```{.text include="examples/ch19-formal-techniques/pipe-256/run.out" lines="22-31"}
```

No verdict in five seconds for either property. The memories are gone, and the parent is still not inductive.

**Step 5, the parent's helper.** The tool prints no counterexample to induction (@sec-ch18-trust), so the question of @sec-ch18-helper is asked by hand: from which unreachable state could `P1` fail in one step? From one where `G` is zero while a child's ghost count is not, so that the pipe is not empty although its own count says it is. Nothing in the parent ties `G` to the children's counts. Say so: `G` is the sum of the two ghost counts, each at most 256. Induction proves it at once, through the boxes:

```{.text include="examples/ch19-formal-techniques/pipe-256/run.out" lines="32-40"}
```

**Step 6, the properties under the helper.** With the helper assumed, both properties are proven, and the two shallow witnesses are reached again under the final assumptions; a second run, by bounded search with two minutes, reaches `P2`'s own antecedent, the pipe full, at depth 513:

```{.tcl include="examples/ch19-formal-techniques/pipe-256/pipe.tcl" lines="95-112"}
```

```{.text include="examples/ch19-formal-techniques/pipe-256/run.out" lines="41-64"}
```

**Step 7, a mutant.** One child built from the FIFO whose count wraps one push short of full, the mutant of @sec-ch19-initval. The child's ghost helper catches it, by bounded search, at depth 256: the ghost count and the mutant's count part company at the wrap.

```{.text include="examples/ch19-formal-techniques/pipe-256/run.out" lines="65-68"}
```

**Step 8, the record.** The script prints it last, one line per verdict with its step, engine and limit, and one line per assumption with the row that discharges it:

```{.text include="examples/ch19-formal-techniques/pipe-256/run.out" lines="69-87"}
```

Read as a sentence for a verification plan: `P1_A` and `P2_A` are proven at 256 entries by induction on the pipe with both FIFOs boxed, under the children's contracts `CE` and `CF` and the parent's helper `HP`; each contract is proven on one FIFO by induction under the ghost helper `H`, which is proven alone; `HP` is proven by induction under the contracts; the witnesses `Drain_C` and `Both1_C`, and `Full_C`, `P2`'s own antecedent, are reached under the final assumptions, and `U1Full_C` on the boxed pipe; a mutant child is caught by `H_A` at depth 256. Nothing in the record depends on a run that ended without a verdict, and every run that did is listed. @fig-ch19-pipe draws the structure with its verdicts.

![The worked example: the pipe of two 256-entry FIFOs, each boxed under its contract on its ghost count, the parent's helper tying the pipe's count to the two, and the verdict of each step of the `pipe-256` example.](../figures/ch19-pipe.svg){#fig-ch19-pipe fig-alt="Two gray boxes, FIFO u0 and FIFO u1, in series, each with a small ghost register g beside it and a contract label: empty iff g == 0, full iff g == 256. Above them the parent's ghost count G with the helper: G == u0.g + u1.g, each at most 256. Below, a strip of verdict cells for steps 1 to 7: covers reached at depths 4, 3 and 258; child helper and contract proven; parent properties without the helper no verdict; parent helper proven; P1 and P2 proven, with covers reached at depths 4, 3 and 513; mutant child refuted at depth 256."}

::: {.callout-note title="Worked Example"}
The procedure, for a design too large to prove flat. (1) Write witness covers and run them by bounded search on the design as it will be proved; where a natural witness is deep, choose shallower ones that exercise each term of the properties for the first look, and give the deep one its own run and limit, or record it as not reached. (2) Prove each child's contract on the child, stated on its ports and on ghost state built from its ports, with whatever helper the child needs. (3) Box the children and assume their contracts. (4) Run a proving engine on the parent with a limit. (5) On no verdict, ask what unreachable state a step could start from, write the reason as a helper over the parent's and the children's ghost state, and prove it. (6) Assume the helper, prove the properties, and run the covers again under the final assumptions, the deep one included. (7) Plant a mutant in a child and check that some property catches it. (8) Write the record: every property with its engine and assumptions, every assumption with the row that discharges it, every cover with its depth, and every limit that ended without a verdict.
:::

How much did the abstractions buy, in time? This book's rule is that seconds appear only in a table that carries its date and is regenerated by a script. The example `seconds-ric3`, which needs rIC3, runs the rows of this chapter that ended in a proof, one property and one engine at a time:

{{< include /examples/ch19-formal-techniques/seconds-ric3/tbl-seconds.md >}}

Read it for orders of magnitude. Through the box and the contract, the memory property is proved in hundredths of a second, and the side condition the abstraction left, the contract with its helper, costs far more than the property did: the work moved, and did not vanish. The pipe's properties with the parent helper cost about as little; without it, rIC3 needed noticeably longer, boxed or flat. The case split's four cases add up to about the whole.

## Future directions {#sec-ch19-future}

::: {.callout-important title="Future Directions"}
Four directions are visible from this chapter's examples, and the chapter claims no result for any of them. The manual loop of boxing, reading a spurious trace and restoring logic is what counterexample-guided abstraction refinement automates [@clarke2000cegar]; an open tool that ran it on RTL would turn the first family of the catalog from a craft into a command. Proof-core coverage (@sec-ch19-core) is available today only as a vendor feature, and an open implementation would let a reader ask which logic a proof in this book actually used. The two-word check failed where a proof needed a fact about every slot of a memory at once; engines that learn such quantified invariants over arrays would close that gap without a hand-written helper. And the proof record of the worked example is a list of claims a reviewer must take on trust; a record whose every line a small independent program can re-check, extending the certificates of @sec-ch18-trust from one engine's invariant to a whole decomposition, would make a compositional proof a different kind of evidence. Proposing helpers and contracts is also the kind of step that @sec-ch34 discusses handing to a program, with the property checker as the judge of each proposal.
:::

## Summary {#sec-ch19-summary}

- Every change to a verification problem keeps proofs (it adds behaviors), keeps counterexamples (it removes behaviors), or keeps both (the property cannot see it); a cover runs the other way. Know which before reading a verdict, and record every side condition a change leaves.
- A black box, a cut point and a timer abstraction remove logic and keep proofs. Their counterexamples are often spurious, and each spurious trace asks for a line of contract, which is then proved on the real logic. A boxed module's own assertions stay listed as errors and are not checked.
- A RAM of 256 words, with no verdict from induction whole, was proven through one symbolic slot and a contract; the contract was proven on the storage with one helper. A bug 255 pushes from reset was found at depth 1 from invariant states, with the invariant proven at reset and inductive.
- The spelling `$anyconst` left no RTL property in the report and printed nothing; a free input held by `$stable` works, and binds the reset cycle too. One tracked word, with a slot helper, proved the FIFO's data integrity; two tracked words proved order only in the position form with slot helpers, and the flag form's once-only checks need a quantified invariant no engine learned.
- A rotation proved to be a symmetry of the arbiter, with a free start that covers reset, let one port's proof stand for four; with `last` reset to 3 the same check failed at depth 2, and fixed priority failed ports 1 to 3 outright.
- Ghost state and history variables add logic that only reads the design, and keep both answers. A protocol checker with a role parameter serves both sides of a link; bound in the wrong role it proved a false rule about the input, shown only by an unreachable cover. A prophecy asserted before it is checked failed at depth 1 on a correct FIFO.
- Assume-guarantee is sound for safety when a register breaks every loop and each block is proved alone, with its neighbor removed, and the flat ring agreed; on one ring with both resets at 1, the two lemmas, each assumed in the other's proof, were both proven and both false; for liveness the ring was refuted by a lasso in which neither block ever starts. A case split needs its completeness check, which alone caught a forgotten case. A hierarchical contract must be stated on ports.
- On the DMA, an end-to-end property followed from two lemmas at once, and the lemmas had no verdict from any engine: the chain was sound, and the work was in its first links.
- A generic deep cover passed a dead end that only some traces met; the assertion's own witness cover caught it. Three mutants were each killed, by different properties, and the FIFO's occupancy checker alone missed both data mutants.
- Two control properties of a pipe of two 256-entry FIFOs were proven by induction through boxes, contracts and one parent helper, each assumption discharged in the record. @fig-ch19-map is the catalog to return to.

## Exercises {#sec-ch19-exercises}

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise"}
1. For each change, say whether proofs, counterexamples or both survive: (a) box a module; (b) add `assume {!req}`; (c) replace an address by a free input held by `$stable`; (d) set `DEPTH` from 256 to 4.
2. In the output of `mem-abs`, the boxed run without a contract reports a counterexample at depth 3. Is the memory wrong? Which line of the output says that the trace may be spurious, and what removes it?
3. The wrap mutant is found at depth 1 from invariant states in `init-value`. Which fact makes a proof from those states a proof from reset, which row of the output proves it, and what does the second `INV_A` row add? Why is the depth-0 counterexample of the weaker start set not a bug?
4. A colleague's FIFO proof reports only the shell's assumptions after they added `$anyconst` to the wrapper. What happened, and what spelling does the tool accept?
5. For the four-port round-robin arbiter with `last` reset to 3, give the permutation of ports that maps its transition relation to itself, and say which of the three conditions of a symmetry fails. Under which change does "port 0 proven" cover all four ports, and which rows of `symmetry` support it?
6. From the output of `symmetry`, which ports of the fixed-priority arbiter fail, and at what depth? Give a request pattern that starves port 3.
7. In part D of `protocol`, which row about the input shows that the checker was bound in the wrong role, and why is the proven assertion about the input worthless?
8. From the two-row trace of part C of `history`, explain why the assumption that checks the prophecy does not remove the counterexample.
9. In `ag`, the safety ring's circular argument is sound only if each block is proved alone, with its neighbor removed. Which registers must it also have, and why does the same argument not prove the liveness ring?
10. The case list on `a[7:6]` that omits one case proves every case it has. Which assertion fails, at what depth, and which case is missing?
11. With only "empty exactly when `g` is zero" assumed for each boxed FIFO in `hier`, `P2_A` fails at depth 1. Give the free behavior of a boxed FIFO that the trace must use.
12. In part C of `sanity`, which cover is reached and which is not, and which of the two exposes the assumption?
:::

## Further reading {#sec-ch19-reading}

- Erik Seligman, Tom Schubert and M. V. Achutha Kiran Kumar, *Formal Verification: An Essential Toolkit for Modern VLSI Design*, 2nd ed., Morgan Kaufmann, 2023 [@seligman2023formal].
- Edmund M. Clarke, Orna Grumberg and David E. Long, *Model Checking and Abstraction*, ACM TOPLAS, 1994 [@clarke1994abstraction].
- E. Allen Emerson and A. Prasad Sistla, *Symmetry and Model Checking*, Formal Methods in System Design, 1996 [@emerson1996symmetry].
- Martín Abadi and Leslie Lamport, *The Existence of Refinement Mappings*, Theoretical Computer Science, 1991 [@abadi1991refinement], and *Conjoining Specifications*, ACM TOPLAS, 1995 [@abadi1995conjoining].
- K. L. McMillan, *Circular Compositional Reasoning about Liveness* and *Verification of Infinite State Systems by Compositional Model Checking*, both CHARME 1999 [@mcmillan1999circular; @mcmillan1999compositional].
- Jerry R. Burch and David L. Dill, *Automatic Verification of Pipelined Microprocessor Control*, CAV 1994 [@burch1994pipelined].
- Armin Biere and Daniel Kroening, *SAT-Based Model Checking*, in the *Handbook of Model Checking*, Springer, 2018 [@bierekroening2018sat].
